notes.1: Candidates were generally able to write the correct arrival time of the ferry.
notes.3: This question was generally correct, although a small number of candidates misread the question and gave the probability of a student going by bus rather than not going by bus.
notes.4: Few candidates scored both marks on this question. However, many earned 1 mark for either 4 x or –3. A small minority wrote an expression rather than an equation by omitting the left hand side.
notes.5: Very few candidates were able to correctly answer this question. Despite the question paper stating the diagram was not to scale, it was evident that some candidates had attempted to measure the angle. The common error was to subtract 107 from 180 and give the answer 73.
notes.7: Stronger candidates often scored full marks on this question. Weaker candidates who did not understand percentage reduction just subtracted 15300 from 17000.
notes.9: Well attempted with many candidates scoring at least 1 mark for writing π r = 19.7. Several went on to score full marks. Common errors were to use π d or to just find the square root of 19.7.
notes.11: Stronger candidates were able to answer this question using a full method. Some candidates realised that the angle on the right was 20°; this was often written on the diagram and scored 1 mark. Many candidates just wrote an incorrect number on the answer line without any method to indicate where the answer had come from, so could gain no credit.
notes.13: Several candidates showed clear, correct answers. Most attempted elimination, but errors often occurred by not consistently adding all the terms when y was to be eliminated, or subtracting when x was eliminated. Some candidates became confused by subtraction with negative numbers and wrote -3 y rather than − 11 y.
notes.15: A very well answered question with candidates being slightly more successful in part (b) than part (a). ⎛ 4 ⎞ ⎛ 0 ⎞ ⎜ ⎟ ⎜ ⎟ − 9 28 ⎝ ⎠ ⎝ ⎠
notes.16: The lines of symmetry were correct more often than the rotational symmetry. Several candidates only attempted to answer the lines of symmetry, while others gave the order of rotational symmetry as an angle (90° etc) rather than as a number.
notes.general_comments: In general the candidates showed a good level of knowledge and understanding when attempting the paper. For the majority of candidates time was not an issue. Candidates were weakest on equations of lines, bearings, angles and converting square centimetres into square metres. Topics which were answered well included time calculations, ordering fractions, decimals and percentages, and negative numbers. The majority of candidates showed working, but the importance of showing working must be stressed to all candidates, as some lost marks due to writing answers only. Candidates should show their working below the question as instructed on the front of the paper.
notes.2a: Most candidates ordered the numbers correctly.
notes.2b: About half the candidates chose the correct expression. 4 1 9 3
notes.6a: Weaker candidates subtracted 2 from 5 instead of 5 from -2.
notes.6b: The difference between -2 and 11 was generally correctly found.
notes.8a: Many candidates were able to collect the expressions together, but did not score the mark as they had not written “= 52”. It is important that candidates read the question carefully and fully answer the question.
notes.8b: Many candidates who answered part (a) correctly went on to score both marks here. Of those who did not, many scored 1 mark for getting either 4 x or 56.
notes.10a: The majority of candidates were able to answer this question correctly. The most common error was writing p .
notes.10b: This part was less well answered than part (a) although many candidates did score both marks. n 6 6 or kq . A common error was 4 . Several other candidates scored 1 mark for either 4 q 7 6
notes.12a: Several candidates were able to correctly answer this question. Common incorrect answers were 100 and -100, not appreciating the meaning of the negative index.
notes.12b: This part of the question was the part which more candidates were able to do, with many correct answers seen.
notes.12c: Many correct answers were seen. It appeared that not all candidates had or knew how to use a calculator. Common incorrect answers were 55.56…, apparently from multiplying 343 by 3.
notes.14a: This part was the best attempted of this question, with many correct answers.
notes.14b: This was the least well answered part. Many candidates appeared not to realise triangle COA was isosceles.
notes.14c: Many candidates appeared not to know angle CAB was a right angle.
notes.14d: Many were successful in this part, either by giving the correct answer or following through from their answer to part (c).
notes.17ai: by 60. Some candidates did not realise they had to multiply by 60.
notes.17aii: Many scored the mark in this part for either the correct answer or for multiplying their answer to part (a)
notes.17b: Many fully correct graphs were seen. Some candidates drew the horizontal line correctly but then incorrectly drew the diagonal line. A small number had an incorrect horizontal line but gained the mark for a diagonal drawn to their ( x +15, 0). A small number of candidates had incorrectly read the question and omitted the horizontal line.
notes.18a: A significant number of candidates appeared to be unfamiliar with factorising, as many did not attempt to answer this question.
notes.18b: This part was more successful than part (a) and was attempted by more candidates. Many scored 1 mark for correctly multiplying out one bracket. Errors were than made by adding unlike terms or confusion with squaring. Some weaker candidates added the term in front of the bracket rather than multiplying. 2 2
notes.19ai: There were many correct answers, although 75 cm was frequently seen, even though the number of tiles was asked for.
notes.19aii: Many candidates did not understand they needed to multiply their answer to part (a) by 10. Several candidates multiplied by 25.
notes.19bi: The area of one tile was generally correctly calculated.
notes.19bii: Very few candidates were able to convert from square cm to square m correctly. Common errors were to divide by 100 or 1000, while others multiplied.
